content.passage: Every fall, several billion birds leave their breeding grounds in northern Europe and Asia. They travel south without passports or awareness of the borders they cross. Many of them fly directly over Egypt. Their route is so reliable that birdwatchers can predict, almost to the week, when the sky above certain wetlands will fill with birds. The journey is staggering by any measure. A single Eurasian curlew may cover several thousand kilometers in just a few weeks. It depends on a chain of wetlands, river deltas, and coastal marshes, and each one belongs to a different country, with its own laws and priorities. If a single link in that chain disappears because a wetland is drained for agriculture, built over for housing, or simply left too polluted to support the insects and fish that migratory birds depend on — the consequences are felt not by the country that made the decision, but by ecosystems thousands of kilometers away that never had any say in the matter.
